papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models show promising potential in text generation tasks, but are prone to problems such as text repetition, semantic drift, and generation quality degradation when the generation length exceeds the training length. To address these challenges, we propose RangeSWA, a training-free length extrapolation method. The method combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local details and support long-range context access. In addition, generation degradation caused by length extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling. We conducted experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models, and the results show that RangeSWA can effectively reduce generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.

Uses local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to balance local detail with long-range context.
Applies positional remapping, conditioning-attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling to mitigate extrapolation degradation.
Experiments across multiple continuous diffusion language models show reduced perplexity and text repetition in long-text generation.

papers.abstract: The order in which tokens are predicted in language modeling has a profound impact on the quality of generated sequences. Autoregressive and masked diffusion models iteratively fill in tokens and can exploit such orderings across generation steps, but how to leverage an ordering for one-step parallel language modeling is unclear. We introduce asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs), which incorporate prediction order into one-step modeling by learning the flow maps of asynchronous flows. These flows specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. We formulate a general class of asynchronous flows that admit both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new methods for their flow map distillation. The resulting models can generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering encoded in the flow into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.
bullets: Addresses how token ordering can improve one-step parallel language modeling.
Uses tokenwise time schedules to control relative denoising progress across tokens.
Supports both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive asynchronous schedules.
Introduces flow-map distillation methods so models internalize ordering in their hidden states.
Achieves state-of-the-art one-step results on Sudoku solving and GSM8K code generation.

papers.abstract: Online Temporal Action Localization (OnTAL) aims to detect and localize action instances from untrimmed streaming videos in real time. Unlike offline approaches, OnTAL models have no access to future frames and cannot go back and refine earlier predictions, which makes the task considerably harder given the strict real-time constraints and narrow temporal window available. Most existing OnTAL methods lean on either brief anchor-based context or a single-scale memory of past frames, which limits how well they can capture actions unfolding across multiple time scales or requiring long-range reasoning in Procedural Videos. To address these gaps, we present DUGO (Dual-Scale Encoding and Gaussian Memory Online), a new OnTAL framework that jointly models local motion dynamics and long-range temporal dependencies. At its core, DUGO uses a Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder, pairing depth-wise local representations with global self-attention so it can pick up both fine-grained temporal patterns and broader contextual cues. We also introduce a Gaussian Memory Bank, which represents action memory as stochastic, input-conditioned Gaussian prototypes, allowing for richer temporal memory through gated cross-attention applied at both the encoder and anchor-query stages. Extensive experiments on procedural egocentric datasets (EGTEA, EPIC-Kitchens-100) demonstrate that DUGO achieves state-of-the-art performance while also providing substantial improvements on non-egocentric benchmarks such as Muses. The project page is available at: https://aman554-eq.github.io/DUGO
bullets: Targets Online Temporal Action Localization without access to future frames or the ability to revise past predictions.
Uses a Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder to capture both fine-grained motion and long-range temporal context.
Introduces an input-conditioned Gaussian Memory Bank with gated cross-attention at encoder and anchor-query stages.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on EGTEA and EPIC-Kitchens-100, with improvements on the non-egocentric Muses benchmark.

papers.abstract: Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.
bullets: Improves the teacher’s success on RoboTwin from 33.4% to 63.6% through recursively proposed and statistically tested harness edits.
Distills teacher trajectories, reasoning, and recovery behavior into a compact 4B student using the fixed evolved harness.
The final student reaches 62.8% on RoboTwin, and students generally remain close to their corresponding teachers across four harness versions.
Evolved harnesses transfer to other frozen planners without retraining and outperform several open 4B/27B comparison agents on identical episodes.
On three unseen benchmarks, the student performs close to a 552B planner using the same harness, within the reported evaluation scope.

Stage 2: after evolution ends, we freeze H∗ and collect teacher trajectories, including reasoning and recovery branches. These are mixed with offline real-robot supervision to train tiny students (0.8B–4B), which replace the teacher in the same harness. Evaluation covers three training domains and three unseen benchmarks, plus three closed-loop real-robot tasks on an SO-ARM101 arm.

papers.abstract: Deformable linear objects (DLO) pose a coupled perception and control challenge: their slender geometry makes precise localization difficult, while their deformations depend on object-specific physical properties. To address this challenge, we propose PS-DLO, a property- and spatially aware DLO manipulation policy. First, contrastive image-text learning maps the initial observation to categorical descriptions of DLO properties, providing explicit physical and structural priors for action generation. Second, SAM3 extracts mask-guided features from future observations, which are distilled into the policy's action expert to encode task-relevant DLO regions and their subsequent configurations. We evaluate PS-DLO on nine real-world tasks across single-arm and bimanual platforms, training a shared multi-task policy for each embodiment. PS-DLO achieves an average success rate of 68.9%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.0 percentage points. In generalization experiments, PS-DLO achieves higher success rates than the baseline in six of seven visual-shift conditions on butterfly-knot untying. These results demonstrate that combining object-property priors with future spatial supervision improves multi-task DLO manipulation and robustness to visual variation.
bullets: Addresses the coupled perception and control challenges caused by DLO geometry and object-specific deformation.
Uses contrastive image-text learning to infer categorical physical and structural properties from the initial observation.
Uses SAM3 mask-guided features from future observations, distilled into the action expert to highlight relevant regions and configurations.
Evaluated across nine real-world tasks on single-arm and bimanual platforms with shared multi-task policies.
Achieves 68.9% average success, 20.0 percentage points above the strongest baseline, and outperforms it in six of seven visual-shift conditions for butterfly-knot untying.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of PS-DLO. The framework consists of DLO property extraction and future spatial knowledge distillation. The property extractor maps the initial observation to a categorical property description for policy conditioning, while the distillation branch uses SAM3-guided features from future observations to provide spatial supervision for the action expert through a teacher–assistant scheme. Training proceeds in three stages: contrastive propertyextractor adaptation, teacher pretraining with auxiliary action supervision, and joint training with teacher–student alignment.

(b) Image downsampling degrades fine details of slender DLO while bulky objects remain visually salient, making interaction-relevant regions difficult to localize. These complementary challenges motivate PSDLO, which combines object-property conditioning with future spatial representation supervision to guide action learning.

papers.abstract: Road infrastructure perception is a fundamental component of autonomous driving, as it recovers the structured road elements that define roadway geometry, delimit operational space, and encode traffic regulations. Although individual tasks such as lane detection, drivable-space estimation, traffic-sign recognition, and online map construction have been extensively studied, the field remains fragmented across task definitions, sensing assumptions, output representations, datasets, and evaluation protocols. This survey provides a function-oriented synthesis of road infrastructure perception. We first clarify its scope and organize existing studies into three complementary categories: geometric-structural, functional-spatial, and regulatory-semantic infrastructure. Based on this taxonomy, we review sensing modalities, scene representations, representative methods, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols, emphasizing the field's evolution from image-space recognition toward metric, vectorized, topology-aware, occupancy-based, and rule-grounded scene modeling. We further examine how representation choices affect evaluation and downstream usability, revealing limitations of current benchmarks in relation reasoning, temporal consistency, robustness, and planning-oriented assessment. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions toward unified infrastructure representation, open-environment generalization, relation- and rule-aware reasoning, and downstream-oriented evaluation. By connecting tasks, representations, and evaluation under a common functional framework, this survey aims to establish road infrastructure perception as a coherent foundation for map-compatible and behavior-relevant autonomous-driving scene understanding.
bullets: Organizes infrastructure into geometric-structural, functional-spatial, and regulatory-semantic categories.
Reviews sensing modalities, scene representations, methods, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols.
Traces a shift from image-space recognition toward metric, vectorized, topology-aware, occupancy-based, and rule-grounded modeling.
Identifies benchmark gaps in relation reasoning, temporal consistency, robustness, and planning-oriented evaluation.
Highlights future directions including unified representations, open-environment generalization, rule-aware reasoning, and downstream-focused assessment.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks deployed on smart glasses must adapt to changes in the distribution of incoming data while adhering to strict privacy and device constraints. We present No Frames, Just Frequencies, a bandwidth-efficient source-assisted adaptation framework that characterizes distribution shifts using compact frequency descriptors computed on-device. Rather than transmitting camera frames, the glasses compute and send frequency descriptors to a host device that contains a replica of the model. The host device maps the received frequency descriptor to a distribution shift operator that synthesizes out-of-distribution data and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol. We evaluate the framework on mixtures of ImageNet-C corruptions using convolution-based (ConvNeXtV2-Femto), self-attention-based (DeiT-Tiny), and hybrid (TinyViT-5M) vision models, on person classification (Visual Wake Words), and on object detection (MS-COCO). Our results reveal that adaptation driven solely by the transmitted descriptors recovers $93-95\%$ of the supervised oracle adaptation gain on all three architectures, $82\%$ on Visual Wake Words and $94$--$98\%$ on MS-COCO. Notably, adaptation quality degrades gracefully as the descriptor resolution decreases from $224 $ to $28$ pixels, consistently across architectures, enabling bandwidth reductions from $213\times$ to $784\times$ across the frequency descriptors.
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in on-device vision under strict privacy and bandwidth constraints.
The glasses compute frequency descriptors; a host maps them to shift operators, synthesizes out-of-distribution data, and adapts a model replica.
Evaluated across ImageNet-C, Visual Wake Words, and MS-COCO with convolutional, attention-based, and hybrid vision models.
Descriptor-only adaptation recovers 93–95% of supervised oracle gains across architectures, 82% on Visual Wake Words, and 94–98% on MS-COCO.
Reducing descriptor resolution from 224 to 28 pixels degrades performance gracefully while enabling 213×–784× bandwidth reductions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System overview of the proposed bandwidth-efficient TTA framework. An edge device (i.e., Smart Glasses) computes compact frequency descriptors (RAPSD, DCT, or DWT statistics) from incoming camera frames on-device. Only these descriptors are transmitted to the host device, keeping the per-frame uplink within a low-bandwidth budget instead of streaming raw frames. The host device maps the received descriptor to a synthetic corruption distribution through a sequential pipeline of training corruptions. The host device generates synthetic corrupted data batches from locally stored in-distribution images, and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol [19, 44]. Finally, the updated parameter subset is transmitted back to the edge device.

Figure 5: Descriptors ablation at 224 input resolution: the NFJF adaptation loop re-run with the frequency descriptor replaced by the model-based alternatives. ActStats denotes the first layer and block activation statistics and FeatFinal the pooled pre-logits embedding. Same layout as Fig. 2. ActStats attains the highest adaptation accuracy, improving on DCT by 0.67pp on average and approaching Oracle - CE within 0.71pp. This adaptation gain costs on average 2.3× the DCT payload (a fixed 708B versus architecture-dependent 768–3072B). Computing ActStats requires executing the deployed model’s first layer and block, ≈ 100× the number of DCT FLOPs (∼ 150-180 versus 1.6MFLOPs), whereas the frequency descriptors need no model execution.

Figure 2: Per-architecture accuracy across four input resolutions (28, 56, 112, 224), reported for each frequency descriptor (RAPSD, DCT and DWT). NFJF is compared against three resolution-independent references: No Adapt and Oracle - E baselines and the Oracle - CE empirical upper bound. Bars report the mean over the 63 test DAGs of ImageNet-C; error bars indicate ±𝜎 . Oracle - E accuracy markedly improves on NoAdapt only for ConvNeXtV2-Femto and destabilizes on DeiT-Tiny and TinyViT-5M, confirming the fragility of unsupervised entropy-based adaptation under distribution shift. NFJF accuracy improves on No Adapt across all three architectures for resolutions > 28 and it surpasses Oracle - E at all resolutions on DeiT-Tiny and TinyViT5M. For ConvNeXtV2-Femto, NFJF mostly surpasses Oracle - E at 112 and 224 input resolutions.

Figure 3: Descriptor visualizations under a sample DAG (brightness→ shot noise→ contrast, each at severity 2; Section 5.1), normalized with clean-data statistics. Brightness amplifies the DC component across all descriptors and resolutions; shot noise amplifies high frequencies, an effect that diminishes at lower resolutions since the reduced-scale JPEG decode acts as a low-pass filter. Contrast reduces the midfrequency bands left free by the other two corruptions.

The No Adapt row reports the absolute performance under shift, the common reference of every adaptation gain. The best per-column adaptation gain is reported in bold. The trends observed in Fig. 2 persist: every adaptation gain is positive and approaches the supervised Oracle as the resolution increases, whereas Oracle - E (VWW) collapses below No Adapt.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual-MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long-form Multi-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual-MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross-modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-MSpeaker.

Provides parallel audio and video inputs to assess cross-modal consistency and complementary information use.
Evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs show substantial performance bottlenecks, with tcpWER frequently exceeding 100%.
Highlights fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key open challenges.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer knowledge from large-scale pretraining into robot control, but their manipulation performance remains sensitive to changes in observation conditions, which recent work addresses by fine-tuning the visual module on target-domain data. However, it remains unclear how such adaptation affects robustness beyond the target condition, as existing robustness benchmarks only evaluate models without fine-tuning and adaptation studies only report the target gain. Measuring this cross-dimension effect requires separating target gains from off-target changes, isolating adaptation effects from architectural differences, ruling out generic forgetting, and comparing tuning choices. Therefore, we introduce VLA-Retain, a benchmark that compares five open VLA models, tuned on Camera-view or Sensor-noise data, with their own base checkpoints on LIBERO-Plus dataset spanning seven perturbation dimensions. Our study reveals four findings. First, targeted vision tuning is not local, and its target gain does not predict retention. Mean off-target gain is negative in 8 of 10 model--domain configurations. Under Camera-view tuning, X-VLA gains $69.4$ percentage points on the target but loses $4.6$ points on average elsewhere, whereas OpenVLA-OFT gains $39.3$ and $1.4$ points, respectively. Second, these regressions are not explained only by performance loss on the same tasks without perturbations. Third, broader training coverage raises overall gain over target-specific training but does not eliminate dimension-level regressions. Fourth, tuning strategies are model-dependent, as DELTA-style feature preservation raises X-VLA's mean off-target gain to $+1.2$ points but lowers OpenVLA-OFT's to $-23.1$. Overall, these findings show that target-domain success alone is insufficient and highlight cross-dimensional retention as a key criterion for targeted VLA adaptation.

papers.abstract: Frontier models can control robots through agent harnesses that loop on one question: what motion comes next toward the user's goal? We show that this default loop carries out harmful instructions. With GPT-6 Astra controlling a low-cost SO-101 arm through the Inspect Robots harness on three household tasks whose hazard is common knowledge, such as "put the knife in the toy basket", the policy refused 0% of 15 trials, attempted the harm every time, and completed it in 27%. Its one exit, give_up, is meant for goals that cannot be achieved, and it never cited the hazard. We add an optional runtime safety check to the loop: before the first motion, the model is asked whether it would carry out the instruction, given the same camera frames. The check would have stopped all 15 hazardous instructions, including the 4 that completed the harm, and flagged none of the 15 harmless controls. Code and data: https://github.com/Arnav-Gr0ver/Refuses-When-Asked-Complies-When-Acting.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.
bullets: LLM inference has distinct prefill and decode phases, governed by time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL).
It characterizes configurations using TTFT–ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers, defining parallelism operating regions.
As workloads become more prefill-heavy, the preferred configuration shifts from tensor-parallelism-dominant to pipeline-parallelism-dominant designs.

SLO-aware selection via goodput favors pipeline-dominated configurations under stringent TTFT requirements, while relaxed latency constraints favor tensor-dominated configurations with greater capacity.
For long-context workloads, pipeline-dominated configurations provide more favorable scalability and SLO attainment.

papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of image manipulation techniques has raised growing public security concerns. Existing Image Forgery Localization (IFL) methods can accurately localize manipulated regions but are often unable to adapt to newly emerging forgeries. In real-world forensic scenarios, data typically arrive sequentially, yet continual model adaptation remains largely unexplored in IFL. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first continual learning framework for IFL and establish a comprehensive benchmark under two realistic data-evolution protocols: cross-dataset and cross-content continual learning. Evaluations of representative state-of-the-art IFL and continual learning methods reveal substantial performance degradation, highlighting two key challenges: (1) adaptively capturing intrinsic forensic traces from incoming data across unseen domains, and (2) preserving previously acquired forensic knowledge during sequential adaptation. To address these challenges, we propose a forensic-aware continual adaptation framework. First, a forensic trace mining module employs Spatial Mixture-of-Forensic-Experts (SMoFE) to dynamically route complementary forensic cues across spatial locations, together with Forensic Evidence-Guided Dense Prompting (FEGDP) to transform low-level forensic traces into structured localization evidence for SAM. Second, Fisher-weighted LoRA Gradient (FLAG) surgery identifies old-task-sensitive adaptation directions and suppresses conflicting updates, mitigating catastrophic forgetting while preserving plasticity for emerging forgery domains. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both pixel-level forgery localization and image-level forgery detection across diverse continual learning scenarios.
bullets: Introduces the first continual learning framework and benchmark for image forgery localization under cross-dataset and cross-content data evolution.

Applies FLAG surgery to suppress updates that conflict with old-task knowledge, reducing catastrophic forgetting while preserving adaptation.

papers.abstract: LLM agents performing long-horizon tasks accumulate tool results that later steps may need. Passing the full history to every invocation is costly even when it fits within the context window, while reducing it risks omitting needed information. Existing context management methods can overlook how earlier tool results are used in subsequent execution, leaving needed information out of context. We introduce ContextRender, which manages context through a persistent graph of execution dependencies. We develop Tool-Flow Analysis to track how later operations reuse information from earlier tool results, providing a signal called observed reuse. A renderer combines this signal with recency and semantic relevance to select results within a fixed history budget, retaining omitted results for later use. Across AppWorld and 8-objective QA with three execution models, ContextRender outperforms the evaluated context management baselines using a 6K history budget, well below the models' maximum context windows. Within this budget, it achieves task performance close to or above that of passing the full history while reducing mean inference cost by 10.2%-32.2% relative to Full history. Ablations show that observed reuse improves task performance and retention of results reused later.
bullets: Full-history context is costly, while aggressive reduction can omit information needed by later steps.
It maintains a persistent execution-dependency graph and uses Tool-Flow Analysis to estimate observed reuse of prior tool results.
A renderer combines observed reuse with recency and semantic relevance under a fixed history budget, while retaining omitted results for possible later use.
Across AppWorld and 8-objective QA with three execution models, it outperformed evaluated baselines using a 6K history budget.

papers.abstract: Multi-step visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers complex questions by repeatedly retrieving visual evidence, updating an intermediate state, and deciding whether to continue searching or answer. Yet retrieving relevant evidence does not ensure its effective use throughout the reasoning trajectory. As multi-step reasoning progresses, redundant sources occupy context capacity needed for missing evidence, observations tied to resolved requirements or unproductive searches linger in context, and visual sources are revisited with insufficient detail for fine-grained reading. We term this loss of usable evidence over a reasoning trajectory trajectory-level evidence utilization degradation. To address it, we propose Trajectory-Aware Evidence Coordination (TAEC), a training-free framework that coordinates evidence use around unresolved answer requirements. TAEC tracks these requirements in a shared trajectory state to guide which evidence enters the context, how accumulated memory is retained, and at what level of detail visual evidence is examined. Under a unified evaluation protocol on ViDoSeek, SlideVQA, and MMLongBench-Doc, TAEC achieves the best overall performance against leading training-free visual RAG baselines, with the highest average accuracy across multiple proprietary vision-language models. These results demonstrate that aligning evidence with evolving reasoning needs improves evidence use throughout multi-step visual RAG.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models improve performance on challenging problems by allocating additional computation before answering, but longer reasoning does not always lead to better results and can introduce substantial redundant reasoning on simple problems. Conversely, aggressively shortening reasoning can degrade performance on difficult ones. Effective reasoning therefore requires dynamically deciding when additional computation is useful based on the reasoner's capabilities and evolving solution state. Existing approaches often rely on predefined budgets or intervention rules, retrain the target reasoner, or require additional supervision. We introduce MetaCtrl, a lightweight controller that adaptively regulates a frozen reasoner without predefined token budgets or reasoner retraining. We formulate reasoning regulation as a sequential metacognitive control problem: MetaCtrl observes the evolving reasoning trace and decides whether to continue, simplify, skip redundant steps, or conclude reasoning. It is trained directly with reinforcement learning using a reward that prioritizes correctness while favoring shorter trajectories among correct solutions, requiring neither supervised intervention trajectories nor problem-specific budgets. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and code, MetaCtrl consistently improves the accuracy of LRMs while reducing their reasoning length. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, it improves average accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing generation length by 53.3%. Without further training, the same controller transfers to an unseen reasoner (e.g., Qwen3-14B), improving average accuracy by 2.9 points and reducing generation length by 50.3%. These results establish MetaCtrl as a plug-and-play controller for improving reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing inference-time generation. The code is available at https://github.com/binbin2xs/MetaCtrl.

papers.abstract: Non-injective mappings in neural networks map distinct inputs to the same representation, thereby implicitly inducing equivalence relations in the input space. However, the input differences eliminated by these mappings may still be required by downstream tasks, creating a mismatch between operator-induced indistinguishability and task-required distinctions. For non-injective linear operators realized in the current forward pass, their null spaces exactly characterize these invisible input variations. We propose Task-Relevant Null-Space Residuals (NSR), a general residual framework for non-injective linear mappings. NSR combines null-space component extraction from pre-mapping representations, member-level encoding and gating, and application-specific integration to exploit potentially task-relevant information under downstream supervision while preserving the original aggregation or merging rules. We evaluate NSR in two structurally different settings: token merging and graph aggregation. In token merging, NSR achieves higher semantic segmentation performance than the corresponding compressed baselines in 34 out of 36 evaluated configurations, with a maximum observed gain of 31.51 mIoU points under strong compression. In graph aggregation, NSR achieves 100% training accuracy on Tree-NeighborsMatch at depths d=2--6 across three backbones, alongside gains on heterophilic node classification and molecular graph regression. Together, these results support null-space residuals as a practical complement to non-injective linear mappings, enabling downstream models to learn from input distinctions invisible in the original operator's output.

For graph aggregation, it reaches 100% training accuracy on Tree-NeighborsMatch at depths 2–6 across three backbones and improves other graph tasks.
